drivers.name: mock
families: any device file for testing and demos
drivers.tests: reference driver for the conformance suite

estimate.devices: none (simulation only)
estimate.reasoning: The mock driver never talks to hardware. It runs any device file in memory for tests, demos and the website playground.

drivers.name: ble
families: DIY ESP32, nRF52 and Pico W peripherals
drivers.tests: fake BleakClient and BleakScanner with a simulated Environmental Sensing peripheral

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: Any BLE peripheral whose characteristics use standard formats can be described in a device file, and describe() maps the SIG Environmental Sensing and Battery services automatically. Billions of BLE devices ship each year, but many use encrypted or undocumented vendor protocols, so the realistic count is the devices with standard services or a documented GATT table, which is still thousands of models.

drivers.name: esphome
protocols: ESPHome native API over TCP, plaintext or Noise encrypted
families: ESP32, ESP8266, RP2040 and BK72xx boards running ESPHome
sensors, switches, lights, fans, numbers, selects and buttons defined in ESPHome YAML
drivers.tests: native API simulator over a local TCP socket, driven by the real aioesphomeapi client

estimate.devices: every ESPHome node, hundreds of thousands of installs
estimate.reasoning: ESPHome is the most common firmware for DIY ESP-based devices and is preinstalled on a growing set of commercial products under the Made for ESPHome program. Every node speaks the same native API, and the driver maps the common entity types without per-device code.

drivers.name: firmata
families: ESP8266 and ESP32 with Firmata over serial
drivers.tests: StandardFirmata simulator over a simulated port and a real pty

estimate.devices: tens of board models, millions of units
estimate.reasoning: StandardFirmata ships with the Arduino IDE and runs on every AVR Arduino board and most compatible clones. The firmata/arduino Boards.h file lists support for roughly forty board families, including Teensy and ESP boards. What is attached to the pins is up to the device file.

drivers.name: hid
protocols: Bluetooth HID through the operating system
families: custom HID gadgets on RP2040, ESP32-S2/S3 and ATmega32U4 boards
drivers.tests: fake hidapi module with a simulated macropad and a real report descriptor

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: HID needs no vendor driver on Linux, macOS and Windows, so it is the default class for small USB input and indicator devices and for homemade gadgets built with TinyUSB or the Arduino HID library. Any device whose report layout is documented or readable from its report descriptor can be described in a device file. Keyboards and mice that the operating system claims exclusively, and devices that need a vendor command protocol on top of HID, are not covered.

drivers.name: homeassistant
families: Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter and Wi-Fi devices that Home Assistant integrates
drivers.tests: Home Assistant simulator over an HTTP mock transport and a real local WebSocket server

estimate.devices: tens of thousands of device models, through more than two thousand integrations
estimate.reasoning: Home Assistant lists over two thousand integrations, and each brand integration covers many models. Every device Home Assistant shows as a light, switch, fan, number, select, sensor or binary sensor entity works through this bridge with no extra code. Zigbee, Z-Wave and Matter devices are reached the same way.

drivers.name: http
families: lab and bench gadgets with REST APIs
DIY ESP32 and Pico W web servers
drivers.tests: httpx.MockTransport with a simulated smart plug

estimate.devices: unbounded, at least tens of thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: Any device with a documented local HTTP API can be described in a device file without new code. Shelly alone documents a local HTTP API for its whole Gen1 and Gen2 range, Tasmota exposes an HTTP command endpoint on every flashed device, and most microcontroller web server sketches speak JSON over HTTP. The count is limited only by devices that need a protocol other than HTTP or a login flow the driver does not support.

drivers.name: marlin
protocols: Marlin G-code over USB serial, with line numbers and checksums
families: pen plotters and other Marlin machines
drivers.tests: Marlin protocol simulator over a simulated port and a real pty

estimate.devices: hundreds of printer models, millions of units
estimate.reasoning: Marlin ships on most consumer FDM printers (Creality, Prusa before Buddy, Anycubic, Artillery, Sovol and many kit printers) and its configuration repository lists several hundred board and printer configurations. Forks that keep the host protocol (Prusa Firmware for the MK3) also work for temperatures, targets, fan and homing.

drivers.name: midi
protocols: MIDI 1.0 over DIN through an interface
families: control surfaces with LEDs and motorised faders
drivers.tests: fake mido backend with a simulated pad controller, real mido messages

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: Every class-compliant USB MIDI device works without a vendor driver on Linux, macOS and Windows, and MIDI 1.0 has been the standard for controllers and instruments since 1983. Any device whose MIDI implementation chart lists its CCs and notes can be described in a device file. Devices that only work through vendor SysEx are not covered.

drivers.name: modbus
drivers.tests: pymodbus server with a simulated fan controller, TCP and RTU framing

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: Modbus has been the default fieldbus for meters, drives and controllers since 1979 and is an open standard maintained by the Modbus Organization. Almost every vendor of energy meters, VFDs, PID controllers and inverters publishes a Modbus register map, and any device with a published map can be described in a device file without new code. Devices that only speak a vendor extension on top of Modbus are not covered.

drivers.name: moonraker
families: Klipper 3D printers (Voron, RatRig, Creality K1 and Sonic Pad, Sovol SV08, Elegoo Neptune 4, Qidi)
drivers.tests: Moonraker simulator over an HTTP mock transport and a real local WebSocket server

estimate.devices: every Klipper install with Moonraker, hundreds of printer models
estimate.reasoning: Moonraker is the API server that Mainsail and Fluidd need, so practically every Klipper printer runs it. Klipper's config folder ships several hundred printer and board configurations, and several vendors now ship Klipper with Moonraker from the factory.

drivers.name: mqtt
families: ESPHome and Shelly devices with MQTT enabled
drivers.tests: real paho-mqtt client against an in-process MQTT 3.1.1 broker with a simulated fan

estimate.devices: unbounded, at least thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: Any device that publishes state and accepts commands on topics can be described in a device file. Tasmota alone lists over two thousand supported device templates, and Zigbee2MQTT lists several thousand Zigbee devices that it exposes over MQTT with JSON payloads. The driver covers raw and JSON payloads, so devices with binary or protobuf payloads are not covered.

drivers.name: octoprint
families: 3D printers connected to OctoPrint (Marlin, Prusa, RepRapFirmware and Klipper with the OctoPrint connector)
drivers.tests: OctoPrint REST simulator over an HTTP mock transport

estimate.devices: every OctoPrint install, on the order of a hundred thousand active printers
estimate.reasoning: OctoPrint's anonymous usage statistics report on the order of a hundred thousand active instances, each driving one printer, and OctoPrint supports most serial printer firmwares. Anything OctoPrint can control exposes the same REST endpoints, so the driver covers them all at the level of temperatures, fan, homing and job control.

drivers.name: openhal-firmware
protocols: OpenHAL firmware protocol 1 over USB serial or UART
families: maker projects that run the OpenHAL library
drivers.tests: protocol simulator, and the real Arduino library built for the host computer

estimate.devices: any board the Arduino toolchain supports, once it runs the library
estimate.reasoning: The library is plain C++ with no heap and no board-specific code, so it builds wherever the Arduino core provides Stream and millis. It is compile-checked for arduino:avr:uno and esp32:esp32. Coverage grows with every maker who adds it to a sketch, so there is no fixed model count.

drivers.name: rpi-camera
families: Raspberry Pi High Quality and Global Shutter cameras
third-party CSI modules with libcamera support
drivers.tests: fake Picamera2 class built from the picamera2 manual, untested on a real Pi until the hardware plan is run

estimate.devices: tens of camera modules
estimate.reasoning: The official Raspberry Pi camera range is about eight modules, and libcamera supports a few dozen more third-party sensors on the CSI connector. Every one that libcamera can open works through picamera2 the same way, so the driver covers the whole set without per-model code. USB cameras on a Pi use the uvc driver instead.

drivers.name: rpi-gpio
protocols: Raspberry Pi GPIO through gpiozero (lgpio, RPi.GPIO, pigpio)
families: buttons, reed switches and limit switches
drivers.tests: gpiozero's mock pin factory

estimate.devices: every Raspberry Pi with a 40-pin header, and thousands of add-on parts
estimate.reasoning: Every Raspberry Pi since the 2014 B+ has the same 40-pin header with 26 usable GPIO pins, and gpiozero supports all of them including the Pi 5 through lgpio. What hangs off the pins (relays, LEDs, switches, fans, servos) is described in the device file, so any part driven by a digital level, PWM or a servo pulse is covered. Parts that need I2C, SPI or one-wire need other drivers.

drivers.name: scpi
protocols: SCPI over LAN (VXI-11, HiSLIP, raw socket)
drivers.tests: TCP SCPI simulator through PyVISA and pyvisa-py, and pyvisa-sim

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: SCPI has been the standard command language for programmable test equipment since 1990, and every major vendor (Keysight, Rohde and Schwarz, Tektronix and Keithley, Rigol, Siglent, GW Instek, B&K Precision) ships SCPI on its current bench lines. Any of them works with a device file. describe() proposes channels for the common supply, meter, load, generator and scope families from the IDN reply.

drivers.name: serial
protocols: line-based text over USB CDC serial
families: bench instruments with ASCII command sets
drivers.tests: simulated pyserial port and a real pty opened with pyserial

estimate.devices: unbounded, tens of thousands of models in practice
estimate.reasoning: The driver has no built-in command set. Any device whose serial protocol is one text command and one text reply per line can be described in a device file. That covers most hobby microcontroller sketches and a large share of RS-232 lab and industrial equipment. The real limit is how many devices have documented commands, not the driver.

drivers.name: uvc
protocols: USB Video Class 1.1 and 1.5 through V4L2, AVFoundation, Media Foundation or DirectShow
drivers.tests: fake cv2.VideoCapture with a simulated camera, real cv2 JPEG encoding

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: UVC is the class every mainstream USB webcam, microscope camera and capture card implements so that it works without a vendor driver, and the Linux UVC driver alone lists hundreds of tested models. The driver only captures frames, so it works with any of them the operating system can open. Cameras that need a vendor SDK, such as many machine vision cameras, are not covered.

drivers.name: alpaca
drivers.tests: Alpaca server simulator on an httpx mock transport, discovery over local UDP

estimate.devices: hundreds of models, every ASCOM device reachable through ASCOM Remote
estimate.reasoning: Alpaca is the network form of ASCOM, the standard driver interface for astronomy gear on Windows. ASCOM Remote exposes every installed ASCOM driver over Alpaca, and a growing number of mounts, focusers and observatory controllers speak Alpaca natively on Linux and embedded boards. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: grbl
drivers.tests: GRBL 1.1 line protocol simulator over a simulated serial port and a real pty

estimate.devices: hundreds of machine models, most hobby CNC routers and diode lasers
estimate.reasoning: GRBL is the default firmware on Arduino based CNC shields and on most budget CNC routers and diode laser engravers. Many 32-bit controllers run grblHAL, which keeps the same 1.1 line protocol, so the driver covers them as well. The count is a model estimate, not a unit count.

drivers.name: indi
drivers.tests: INDI server simulator on a local TCP port, speaking the XML protocol

estimate.devices: hundreds of models across the INDI driver list
estimate.reasoning: INDI is the device layer of KStars and Ekos, and indiserver ships drivers for most amateur astronomy mounts, focusers, cameras, filter wheels and domes on Linux and the Raspberry Pi. The INDI device list names several hundred supported models. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: lerobot
families: other LeRobot arms with joint goals
drivers.tests: a faithful fake of LeRobot's SOFollower, with each assumption checked in the hardware test plan

estimate.devices: a dozen robot types, thousands of hobby and lab arms built from them
estimate.reasoning: LeRobot registers about a dozen robot types, and the SO-100 and SO-101 kits are among the most built open source arms. The driver reads joint positions and sends joint goals through LeRobot's Robot interface, so it covers robots whose actions are joint positions. Mobile bases and hands with other action types need a map. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: onvif
protocols: ONVIF Profile S and T over SOAP 1.2
drivers.tests: the driver's own SOAP client against a simulated PTZ camera that checks WS-Security digests

estimate.devices: tens of thousands of conformant products
estimate.reasoning: ONVIF lists tens of thousands of conformant products from hundreds of manufacturers, most of them Profile S cameras whose device and media services this driver reads. PTZ moves need a PTZ camera, which is a smaller share. Media2, events, imaging and recording are not covered.

drivers.name: opcua
families: PLCs with an OPC UA server
drivers.tests: asyncua's own OPC UA server running a simulated pump skid

estimate.devices: thousands of controller and instrument models
estimate.reasoning: OPC UA is the standard interface of industrial automation. Most current PLC families include an OPC UA server, and the LADS companion specification brings it to laboratory instruments. The driver reads and changes variables and calls methods, which covers any server that exposes its data that way. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: pylabrobot
drivers.tests: PyLabRobot's LiquidHandler on its chatterbox backend, recorded

estimate.devices: a handful of liquid handler families, each installed in many labs
estimate.reasoning: PyLabRobot drives the Hamilton STAR line, the Tecan EVO and the Opentrons OT-2 through one API. The driver exposes the liquid handling part of that API, so it covers the families PyLabRobot supports for liquid handling. Plate readers, heaters and shakers in PyLabRobot are not covered yet. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: ros2
drivers.tests: rosbridge v2 WebSocket server simulator with a simulated differential drive robot

estimate.devices: hundreds of robot models, any ROS 2 system that runs rosbridge
estimate.reasoning: rosbridge_suite is packaged for every ROS 2 distribution, and most ROS 2 robots expose their state and commands as topics, services and actions it can bridge. The driver reaches a robot through its ROS interface rather than its hardware, so the count follows the ROS 2 robot list. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: sila2
drivers.tests: a thermoshaker served by the sila2 package's own server from feature definitions

estimate.devices: dozens of commercial device families and any custom SiLA 2 server
estimate.reasoning: SiLA 2 is the lab automation standard from the SiLA consortium. Several vendors ship SiLA 2 servers for their instruments, and integrators wrap older instruments with SiLA 2 gateways. The driver reads any feature's properties and runs its commands without generated code, so coverage follows the feature definitions a server offers. The count is a model estimate.

drivers.name: bambu
protocols: Bambu Lab LAN MQTT over TLS, Developer Mode
families: Bambu Lab A1 and A1 mini
drivers.tests: real paho-mqtt client over TLS against a simulated printer on an in-process broker

estimate.devices: about ten printer models
estimate.reasoning: Bambu Lab sells the X1, P1, A1 and newer H2 and P2 families, which share one report format on the local MQTT broker. Bambu Lab documents Developer Mode for X1, P1, A1 and A1 mini, and only printers in that mode accept the commands this driver sends. Reads work in normal LAN mode too. Bambu Lab doesn't publish the message format, so the field list follows community documentation and may miss model-specific fields.

drivers.name: can
protocols: SocketCAN and USB adapters through python-can
families: vehicle and machine buses with documented frames
drivers.tests: python-can virtual bus with a simulated motor drive

estimate.devices: hundreds of documented node types
estimate.reasoning: Any node whose broadcast frames and command frames are documented, or listed in a DBC file, can be described with byte and bit fields. That covers hobby and research motor drives such as VESC and ODrive, many battery management systems, and machines that publish periodic CANopen PDOs or J1939 PGNs. Values that need a request and reply protocol (CANopen SDO, J1939 transport, ISO-TP) are not covered, which leaves out much of the automotive diagnostic world.

drivers.name: knx
drivers.tests: real xknx tunneling against a fake KNXnet/IP server built from xknx's frame classes, with a simulated room

estimate.devices: thousands of certified products
estimate.reasoning: KNX is a single standard across hundreds of manufacturers, and every certified device talks in group telegrams with standard datapoint types, which this driver maps from a group address list. KNX Secure devices and device programming are not covered, and the group addresses must come from the installation's ETS project.

drivers.name: matter
protocols: Matter through the Matter Server WebSocket API
families: Thread devices through a Matter Server
drivers.tests: a WebSocket simulator of the python-matter-server message format with a bulb, a sensor and a thermostat

estimate.devices: thousands of certified products
estimate.reasoning: The Connectivity Standards Alliance lists several thousand certified Matter products, and every one exposes its state as standard cluster attributes, which this driver reads by path. The count is limited to devices a Matter Server can commission and to clusters a device file maps, and was tested only against the python-matter-server message format.

drivers.name: pi-i2c-spi
drivers.tests: fake smbus2 and spidev buses with simulated TMP102, MCP3008 and MCP4921 chips

estimate.devices: hundreds of chip models
estimate.reasoning: Most I2C and SPI sensors, converters and expanders expose fixed-width registers whose values are linear in the reading, which a register map covers. Distributors list thousands of I2C and SPI parts, but chips that need calibration math (BME280, most IMU fusion), SMBus block protocols with a length byte, or multi-step command sequences are not covered, so the estimate counts only the linear register-mapped ones that hobby and lab boards commonly carry.

drivers.name: upnp
families: UPnP AV media renderers and speakers
drivers.tests: async-upnp-client against a fake media renderer with real device and service descriptions and SOAP replies

estimate.devices: thousands of models
estimate.reasoning: UPnP and DLNA are built into most networked speakers, TVs, media servers and home routers, and all of them describe their actions in standard XML that this driver checks maps against. Devices that only implement UPnP for discovery and use a private API for control, and features that need GENA events, are not covered.

drivers.name: zigbee-zwave
protocols: Zigbee through the Zigbee2MQTT MQTT API
Z-Wave through the zwave-js-server WebSocket API
families: Zigbee and Z-Wave thermostats and locks with exposed values
drivers.tests: Zigbee2MQTT simulated on the in-process MQTT broker and a zwave-js-server WebSocket simulator

estimate.devices: several thousand models
estimate.reasoning: Zigbee2MQTT lists several thousand supported Zigbee devices and describes each one's values in its exposes list, which this driver reads directly. zwave-js has device configuration files for a few thousand certified Z-Wave products and reports every value with metadata. The count covers devices those bridges support, not every Zigbee or Z-Wave device sold, and leaves out bridge-only features such as scenes, groups and pairing.
